lesson.title: Running Out at a Constant Clip: The Zero-Order Integrated Rate Law
lesson.summary: The zero-order integrated rate law, [A] = [A]0 - kt, shows that a reactant's concentration falls in a straight line over time because the rate stays constant right up until the reactant runs out.
lesson.body:
Zero order kinetics is the simplest case to turn into an integrated rate law, precisely because the rate itself never changes. Recall from the zero-order reactions chapter that rate = k[A]^0 = k, a fixed number regardless of concentration. Since rate is also defined as -d[A]/dt, this means -d[A]/dt = k, a constant. If concentration is falling at a constant rate with respect to time, then concentration itself must be a straight-line, or linear, function of time, with slope -k. Integrating -d[A]/dt = k over time from the start of the reaction gives the zero-order integrated rate law: [A] = [A]0 - kt, where [A]0 is the initial concentration at t = 0 and [A] is the concentration remaining after time t has elapsed.

This equation is worth comparing directly to the general preview from the integrated rate laws chapter: plotting [A] on the y-axis against t on the x-axis gives a straight line with slope -k and y-intercept [A]0. Of the three basic integrated rate laws, this is the only one where concentration itself, with no logarithm or reciprocal needed, plots as a straight line against time, a direct graphical fingerprint of zero order behavior.

Here is a full worked example. Suppose a catalytic decomposition reaction has been experimentally confirmed to be zero order, with rate constant k = 0.050 M/s and initial concentration [A]0 = 1.00 M. What is [A] after 8.0 seconds? Using the integrated rate law, [A] = [A]0 - kt = 1.00 M - (0.050 M/s)(8.0 s) = 1.00 M - 0.40 M = 0.60 M. Now ask a second question: at what time will the reactant be completely consumed, [A] = 0? Setting [A] = 0 in the same equation gives 0 = 1.00 M - (0.050 M/s)(t), so t = (1.00 M)/(0.050 M/s) = 20 s. As a check, plugging t = 20 s back into the integrated rate law gives [A] = 1.00 M - (0.050 M/s)(20 s) = 1.00 M - 1.00 M = 0.00 M, consistent.

That second calculation carries an important physical warning attached to it. The zero-order integrated rate law predicts a perfectly straight decline in [A], but that decline cannot continue past the point where the reactant is actually gone. In this example, the equation is only physically meaningful for 0 seconds up to 20 seconds. Push t past 20 s and the formula would predict a negative concentration, which is impossible, because once A is used up the true rate has nowhere to go but zero, exactly the caveat raised in the zero-order reactions chapter. In practice, a real zero-order process runs at its constant rate only as long as whatever limits it, a saturated catalyst surface, for instance, still has reactant available to feed it, and then the rate abruptly falls away once the supply is exhausted.
